reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

THE SAME QUESTION AS THE ROW ABOVE WITH THE HANDLE TAKEN OFF, printed so the reader can see which half of that ratio is the address lookup and which half is the observable. Ours mints on a miss (every address here hits) and carries a last-resolved cache, so a body that asks for the same address twice in a row answers the second from a reference comparison — this body cycles through all sixty-four addresses, which defeats that cache deliberately, because a benchmark that hits it every time would price a comparison and call it a lookup.

reading.ours: for (const slot of db.read(bucket)) slot.entity — per member visited
reading.floor: for (const row of set) — per member visited, same container kind
reading.caveat: THE SAME CONTAINER ON BOTH SIDES: an unordered bucket holds its members in a `Set`, so this floor is the structural equal. Ours pays two things the floor does not — the index is settled on every read (deferred filing is what makes a write cheap, and the read is where that debt is collected, here with nothing outstanding) and every member is a slot the consumer must dereference to reach the row, which this body does. The per-read costs — settling and allocating an iterator — are amortised over the hundred-odd members of a bucket, so a caller reading buckets of one pays far more per member than this row shows.

reading.ours: for (const slot of db.read(bucket)) slot.entity — per member visited
reading.floor: for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; i++) — per member visited
reading.caveat: THE SAME OUR-SIDE BODY AS THE ROW ABOVE AGAINST THE FLOOR SOMEBODY WOULD ACTUALLY WRITE. An indexed array walk is the fastest way there is to visit a hundred objects and it beats a `Set` iterator handily, so this ratio is the worse of the two and the more honest answer to "what does reading a group cost me". What the array cannot do is stay correct: nothing maintains it, nothing can be woken by it, and it holds rows rather than identities that outlive them. The gap between this ratio and the `set-iteration` one above is a property of JavaScript containers, not of either design.

Ours settles the index before answering, because a count taken before the frame's deferred filing has run would be last frame's count — that settle is the whole difference and it is charged on every call, with nothing outstanding to settle in this body. The floor reads a field of a container whose correctness is somebody else's problem. Both sides cycle through all sixty-four buckets rather than asking the same one repeatedly.

reading.ours: observable.getValue() on a db.value(slot) built once and held
reading.caveat: THE READ PATH AS THE DOCUMENTATION INTENDS IT: the observable is built outside the clock, once per row, and the timed body only calls it. So this is a closure call and a field read against a variable read. What ours buys over the floor is `onChange` on the same object — the reason a reader can be told rather than polling — which this row does not exercise and does not charge for.

reading.ours: db.value(slot).getValue() — built and thrown away at the read
reading.caveat: THE SAME CALL AS THE ROW ABOVE WRITTEN THE WAY THE DOCUMENTATION SAYS NOT TO, so the gap between the two ratios is the price of building the observable rather than holding it: an object and two closures, per read, all immediately garbage. It is on the table because it is what a render body does when nobody has said otherwise, and because a price nobody can see is a price nobody believes. The allocation debt is collected outside the clock, between samples, so this number is the construction and not the collection of it.

reading.ours: observable.getValue() on a db.field(slot, 'title') built once and held
reading.caveat: A column read through the graph against a property read. Ours goes closure → slot → entity → optional chain → indexed property, and answers `string | undefined` twice over: the identity may carry no value and the value may not carry the column. The floor is one property of an object somebody is holding. What ours buys is that `onChange` here wakes only when THIS column moved, which is the narrowest signal the engine has; the frame group prices what that delivery costs, and this row prices only the read.
